## Why the review looks like this
The half‑precision engine is the cheapest to validate first because it needs the least energy per inference and has the lowest latency, even though its runtime power draw is higher than that of the eight‑bit integer builds.  
The position fine‑tune kept the same half‑precision engine cost but removed the start‑position weakness seen in the original policy, showing clear improvement when the start is shifted left or right; however, at the trained start mark the fine‑tune still does not give enough evidence to claim it is better or worse than the old policy.  
Success rates against the full‑precision reference are so high that both arms sit at or above the ninety‑five percent level, which triggers the pre‑registered ceiling rule that leaves the outcome undecided no matter how many more trials are run unless the rule itself is changed.  
The deliberately miscalibrated builds are stopped by a simple input check that flags any calibration value outside the expected range, so they never reach the arm test.  
The AI judge’s record shows it catches most failures but also produces false alarms on new objects, and because its decision depends only on the final state and is sensitive to wording, it must be re‑validated before anyone relies on its output.  

## Questions to resolve before deployment
- How many trials per arm would be needed to demonstrate that the success difference remains within the allowed tolerance once the pre‑registered ceiling rule is revised?  
- How many trials at the trained start mark are required to move the verdict from undecided to a clear statement about non‑inferiority or superiority?  
- What additional checks on unseen objects and novel scenes are needed to reduce the false‑alarm rate of the AI judge before it can be trusted in deployment?

Success comparisons with the full precision reference cannot be decided yet because both arms sit at or above a high success rate which activates the pre registered ceiling rule leaving the outcome undecided no matter how many more trials are run unless the rule itself is changed.
